simple: several computers settle on one single answer and never change it.
analogy: the friends agreeing on one pizza for Kofi.
precise: a set of processes, each with an input value, must each decide on an output value such that agreement, validity, integrity and termination (below) hold, in a stated failure model.
source: D3 of F5-15 (Michael J. Fischer, Nancy A. Lynch, Michael S. Paterson, "Impossibility of Distributed Consensus with One Faulty Process" (tier 5)); D4 of F5-15 (Martin Kleppmann, "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (tier 3; edition to be recorded)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: nobody decides differently from anybody else.
analogy: Kofi gets one pizza, not two.
precise: no two processes decide different values (the "uniform" form also covers processes that decide and then crash).
source: D4 of F5-15 (Martin Kleppmann, "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (tier 3; edition to be recorded)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the answer was somebody's real suggestion.
analogy: nobody orders a pineapple pizza that no friend asked for.
precise: a decided value was the input (proposal) of some process.
source: D2 of F5-15 (Leslie Lamport, "Paxos Made Simple" (tier 5)); D4 of F5-15 (Martin Kleppmann, "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (tier 3; edition to be recorded)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: each one decides once and does not change its mind.
analogy: no second phone call to the pizzeria.
precise: every process decides at most once.
source: D4 of F5-15 (Martin Kleppmann, "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (tier 3; edition to be recorded)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: everyone who is still working eventually has an answer.
analogy: by Saturday, every friend whose phone works knows the pizza.
precise: every process that does not crash eventually decides some value.
source: D3 of F5-15 (Michael J. Fischer, Nancy A. Lynch, Michael S. Paterson, "Impossibility of Distributed Consensus with One Faulty Process" (tier 5)); D4 of F5-15 (Martin Kleppmann, "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (tier 3; edition to be recorded)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a promise that nothing bad ever happens.
analogy: "Kofi never gets two pizzas".
precise: a property whose violation, if it happens, happens at a definite point of a run and can be shown with a finite prefix of that run (agreement, validity, integrity).
source: D4 of F5-15 (Martin Kleppmann, "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (tier 3; edition to be recorded)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a promise that something good eventually happens.
analogy: "Kofi eventually gets a pizza".
precise: a property that no finite prefix of a run can violate, because the good thing might still happen later (termination).
source: D4 of F5-15 (Martin Kleppmann, "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (tier 3; edition to be recorded)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: more than half of the group.
analogy: two of the three friends.
precise: a set of more than n/2 of the n processes; any two such sets have at least one process in common, which is the fact the protocols of this course rely on.
source: D1 of F5-15 (Diego Ongaro, John Ousterhout, "In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm (Extended Version)" (tier 5)); D2 of F5-15 (Leslie Lamport, "Paxos Made Simple" (tier 5)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: several copies of the same program that stay identical because they perform the same commands in the same order.
analogy: everyone's copy of the shared notebook.
precise: deterministic state machines on several servers that apply the same sequence of commands from a replicated log, so they compute the same states and outputs; consensus keeps the logs identical.
source: D1 of F5-15 (Diego Ongaro, John Ousterhout, "In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm (Extended Version)" (tier 5)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a system where nobody can promise how long a message or a step takes.
analogy: the post can hold a letter for a day or a month, and nobody can tell you which.
precise: a model with no bound on message delay, no bound on relative process speeds and no synchronized clocks; every message is eventually delivered to a non-crashed receiver.
source: D3 of F5-16 (Michael J. Fischer, Nancy A. Lynch, Michael S. Paterson, "Impossibility of Distributed Consensus with One Faulty Process" (tier 5)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a snapshot of the whole system.
analogy: every friend's notes plus every letter still in the post.
precise: the internal state of every process together with the set of messages sent but not yet delivered (the message buffer).
source: D3 of F5-16 (Michael J. Fischer, Nancy A. Lynch, Michael S. Paterson, "Impossibility of Distributed Consensus with One Faulty Process" (tier 5)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: which final answers are still possible from a snapshot.
analogy: "from here, could we still end up with tomato? with mushroom?"
precise: a configuration is 0-valent if every decision reachable from it is 0, 1-valent if every reachable decision is 1, and bivalent if both are reachable.
source: D3 of F5-16 (Michael J. Fischer, Nancy A. Lynch, Michael S. Paterson, "Impossibility of Distributed Consensus with One Faulty Process" (tier 5)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the proof that no fixed rule can always agree and always finish if one computer may stop and messages can be arbitrarily late.
analogy: Priya's theorem about the pizza rules.
precise: in the asynchronous model, no deterministic protocol solves consensus (agreement, validity and termination in every fair run) if even one process may crash.
source: D3 of F5-16 (Michael J. Fischer, Nancy A. Lynch, Michael S. Paterson, "Impossibility of Distributed Consensus with One Faulty Process" (tier 5)); D4 of F5-16 (Martin Kleppmann, "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (tier 3; edition to be recorded)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a run in which nothing is delayed forever, except by a crash.
analogy: every letter is delivered eventually, however late.
precise: an infinite run in which at most one process crashes and every message sent to a live process is eventually delivered.
source: D3 of F5-16 (Michael J. Fischer, Nancy A. Lynch, Michael S. Paterson, "Impossibility of Distributed Consensus with One Faulty Process" (tier 5)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the network is usually well behaved, but you do not know when the bad periods end.
analogy: the post is reliable except during storms, and nobody announces the storms.
precise: a timing model in which bounds on delays and speeds exist or hold eventually but are not known in advance; consensus protocols guarantee termination only in such periods.
source: D4 of F5-16 (Martin Kleppmann, "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (tier 3; edition to be recorded)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the three jobs in Paxos: suggesting, voting, and finding out the result.
analogy: the friend with a new order form; the friends who sign forms; whoever needs to know the final pizza.
precise: proposers issue numbered proposals; acceptors respond to prepare and accept requests and are the processes whose majorities choose a value; learners find out which value has been chosen. One process may play several roles.
source: D2 of F5-17 (Leslie Lamport, "Paxos Made Simple" (tier 5)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a number attached to every attempt, bigger for later attempts.
analogy: the number printed on an order form.
precise: a number from a totally ordered set, unique to one proposer's attempt (for example, a round number combined with the proposer's id); a proposal is a pair (number, value).
source: D2 of F5-17 (Leslie Lamport, "Paxos Made Simple" (tier 5)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: "I will ignore anything older than your number".
analogy: "I'll ignore forms with smaller numbers than yours".
precise: an acceptor's response to prepare(n) when n exceeds every number it has responded to: it promises never to accept a proposal numbered below n and reports the highest-numbered proposal it has accepted, if any.
source: D2 of F5-17 (Leslie Lamport, "Paxos Made Simple" (tier 5)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the value that can never change any more.
analogy: Kofi's pizza, once most friends signed the same form.
precise: a value is chosen when a single proposal with that value has been accepted by a majority of acceptors.
source: D2 of F5-17 (Leslie Lamport, "Paxos Made Simple" (tier 5)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: one friend who is the only one making suggestions.
analogy: the friend who writes the order.
precise: a single proposer selected to issue proposals, so that competing proposers do not keep invalidating each other's ballots; needed for progress, not for safety.
source: D2 of F5-17 (Leslie Lamport, "Paxos Made Simple" (tier 5)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: Paxos repeated for every slot of a log, with one leader doing the first phase once.
analogy: one friend writes the whole week's orders.
precise: the state machine implementation in which a sequence of Paxos instances decides successive log entries and a stable leader executes phase 1 once for all instances it has not yet decided.
source: D2 of F5-17 (Leslie Lamport, "Paxos Made Simple" (tier 5)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a numbered period of time with at most one leader.
analogy: "round 2 of being in charge".
precise: Raft divides time into terms numbered with consecutive integers; each term begins with an election, and at most one candidate wins in a given term; servers exchange their current term in every message and use it as a logical clock to detect stale information.
source: D1 of F5-18 (Diego Ongaro, John Ousterhout, "In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm (Extended Version)" (tier 5)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: listening, asking for votes, in charge.
analogy: the friends who wait for the order; a friend calling a new round; the friend who writes the order.
precise: the three server states of Raft; followers respond to requests, a candidate is a server trying to become leader, and the leader handles all client requests and replicates the log.
source: D1 of F5-18 (Diego Ongaro, John Ousterhout, "In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm (Extended Version)" (tier 5)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how long a follower waits without news before calling an election.
analogy: how long Kofi waits before calling a new round.
precise: a period after which a follower that has received no valid AppendEntries or granted no vote becomes a candidate; Raft chooses it at random from a fixed interval to make split votes rare.
source: D1 of F5-18 (Diego Ongaro, John Ousterhout, "In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm (Extended Version)" (tier 5)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the message "please vote for me".
analogy: "will you let me write the orders this round?"
precise: an RPC sent by candidates carrying the candidate's term, id, last log index and last log term; a server grants at most one vote per term, first come first served, subject to the election restriction.
source: D1 of F5-18 (Diego Ongaro, John Ousterhout, "In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm (Extended Version)" (tier 5)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: an election that nobody wins because the votes were divided.
analogy: Kofi and Lena both call round 2 at the same moment and each gets two yeses.
precise: a term in which several candidates divide the votes so that none reaches a majority; the term ends without a leader and a new election starts after another timeout.
source: D1 of F5-18 (Diego Ongaro, John Ousterhout, "In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm (Extended Version)" (tier 5)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: you only vote for someone whose notebook is at least as up to date as yours.
analogy: you only let a friend write orders if their copy of the shared notebook is not behind yours.
precise: a voter denies its vote if its own log is more up-to-date than the candidate's: the log whose last entry has the later term is more up-to-date; with equal last terms, the longer log is.
source: D1 of F5-18 (Diego Ongaro, John Ousterhout, "In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm (Extended Version)" (tier 5)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: one numbered line of the shared history.
analogy: one numbered line of the shared notebook, with the round in which it was written.
precise: a record holding a state machine command and the term in which the leader received it; its position in the log is its index.
source: D1 of F5-19 (Diego Ongaro, John Ousterhout, "In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm (Extended Version)" (tier 5)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the leader's letter "please add these lines after line k".
analogy: Kofi's letter with new notebook lines.
precise: the RPC by which the leader replicates entries and sends heartbeats; arguments: term, leader id, prevLogIndex, prevLogTerm, entries (empty for a heartbeat), leaderCommit.
source: D1 of F5-19 (Diego Ongaro, John Ousterhout, "In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm (Extended Version)" (tier 5)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: "I only add your lines if my line k matches yours".
analogy: before copying new lines, compare the last shared line's round number.
precise: a follower rejects AppendEntries if its log does not contain an entry at prevLogIndex whose term equals prevLogTerm.
source: D1 of F5-19 (Diego Ongaro, John Ousterhout, "In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm (Extended Version)" (tier 5)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: if two copies agree on a line and its round, they agree on everything before it.
analogy: two notebooks with the same line 4 from round 1 have the same lines 1–4.
precise: if two logs contain an entry with the same index and term, the logs are identical in all entries up through that index.
source: D1 of F5-19 (Diego Ongaro, John Ousterhout, "In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm (Extended Version)" (tier 5)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a line that is safe to act on, because it can never be erased.
analogy: an order that may be phoned to the pizzeria.
precise: an entry is committed once the leader that created it has replicated it on a majority of servers; commitIndex is the highest index known to be committed. Committed entries are durable and will eventually be executed by all available state machines. A leader decides this by counting replicas only for entries of its current term; earlier entries become committed indirectly, behind such an entry (F5-20).
source: D1 of F5-19 and of F5-20 (Diego Ongaro, John Ousterhout, "In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm (Extended Version)" (tier 5)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the leader's two numbers per follower: what to send next, and how much is known to match.
analogy: Kofi's note "Lena: send from line 2; known equal up to line 1".
precise: for each follower, the index of the next entry to send (initialized to the leader's last index + 1) and the highest index known to be replicated on it (initialized to 0).
source: D1 of F5-19 (Diego Ongaro, John Ousterhout, "In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm (Extended Version)" (tier 5)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a new leader always already has every final entry.
analogy: whoever becomes order-writer has every order that was ever phoned to the pizzeria.
precise: if a log entry is committed in a given term, that entry will be present in the logs of the leaders for all higher-numbered terms.
source: D1 of F5-20 (Diego Ongaro, John Ousterhout, "In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm (Extended Version)" (tier 5)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: no two servers ever execute different commands at the same position.
analogy: no two friends ever phone different pizzas for line 2.
precise: if a server has applied a log entry at a given index to its state machine, no other server will ever apply a different log entry for the same index.
source: D1 of F5-20 (Diego Ongaro, John Ousterhout, "In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm (Extended Version)" (tier 5)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a leader never erases or rewrites its own lines.
analogy: the order-writer only adds lines.
precise: a leader never overwrites or deletes entries in its log; it only appends new entries.
source: D1 of F5-20 (Diego Ongaro, John Ousterhout, "In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm (Extended Version)" (tier 5)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the list of servers whose votes count.
analogy: who is in the group chat.
precise: the set of servers participating in the consensus algorithm; Raft stores configurations as special log entries, and a server uses the latest configuration in its log whether or not it is committed.
source: D1 of F5-20 (Diego Ongaro, John Ousterhout, "In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm (Extended Version)" (tier 5)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: during a change, decisions need a majority of the old group and a majority of the new group.
analogy: while friends are joining the chat, an order needs most of the old members and most of the new member list.
precise: a transitional configuration Cold,new in which log entries are replicated to all servers of both configurations and agreement (for elections and commitment) requires separate majorities from Cold and Cnew.
source: D1 of F5-20 (Diego Ongaro, John Ousterhout, "In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm (Extended Version)" (tier 5)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: running the whole distributed system inside one program where time, the network and randomness are fake and controlled.
analogy: replaying the friends' week from a diary, letter by letter.
precise: executing all nodes, the network and the clock in a single process driven by a seeded pseudo-random generator, so that the same seed always produces the same execution.
source: F5-21 lab runs (R1 of F5-21); no source in the F5 registry — definition as used in this course

simple: the part of a test that breaks things on purpose.
analogy: a deliberately bad mail service that loses, delays and duplicates letters and sometimes knocks a friend out.
precise: a component that schedules crashes, restarts, partitions, message loss, delay and duplication during a test run, either at random or targeting specific nodes such as the current leader.
source: F5-21 lab runs (R1 of F5-21); no source in the F5 registry — definition as used in this course

simple: the list of reads and writes that clients made, with when each started and finished and what it returned.
analogy: every member's diary of when they looked into or wrote in a notebook, and what they saw.
precise: a record of operation invocations and responses with their real-time intervals and results; consistency models are defined as conditions on histories.
source: D8 of F5-13 (Maurice P. Herlihy, Jeannette M. Wing, "Linearizability: A Correctness Condition for Concurrent Objects" (tier 5; not in the guide's F5 registry, proposed in this course's notes): definition of linearizability on histories) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open); R1 of F5-13 (university/labs/F5-13/histories.log: Listing 1 on histories.in, g++ (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) 13.3.0, Linux x86_64 cloud build container, exit code 0)

simple: the system behaves as if there were one copy and each operation happened at one instant during its call.
analogy: as if there were only one notebook in the town square, and every reading or writing happened at a single moment while the member was there.
precise: a history is linearizable if there is a total order of its operations that is a legal sequential history of the object and that respects real time: if operation A completed before B was invoked, A precedes B.
source: D8 of F5-13 (Maurice P. Herlihy, Jeannette M. Wing, "Linearizability: A Correctness Condition for Concurrent Objects" (tier 5; not in the guide's F5 registry, proposed in this course's notes): definition of linearizability on histories); D1 of F5-13 (Martin Kleppmann, "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): problems with replication lag (reading your own writes, monotonic reads, consistent prefix reads), leaderless replication and quorums and their limitations, the consistency and consensus chapter (linearizability, its cost, the CAP theorem, ordering guarantees)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: reading an old value after a newer one has been written.
analogy: looking in Chidi's notebook before Amara's letter has arrived.
precise: a read that returns a value older than the latest write that completed before the read began; forbidden by linearizability, allowed by weaker models.
source: D1 of F5-13 (Martin Kleppmann, "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): problems with replication lag (reading your own writes, monotonic reads, consistent prefix reads), leaderless replication and quorums and their limitations, the consistency and consensus chapter (linearizability, its cost, the CAP theorem, ordering guarantees)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: never two leaders in the same term.
analogy: never two friends who both write the order in the same round.
precise: at most one leader can be elected in a given term; it follows from each server voting at most once per term (with the vote kept on stable storage) and a leader needing votes from a majority.
source: D1 of F5-18 (Diego Ongaro, John Ousterhout, "In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm (Extended Version)" (tier 5)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: an empty log entry a new leader adds at the start of its term.
analogy: a blank line the new order-writer writes first, dated with their round.
precise: a log entry with no command that a newly elected leader appends and replicates; once it is committed, all earlier entries are committed too, so the leader learns which entries are committed without waiting for a client command.
source: D1 of F5-20 (Diego Ongaro, John Ousterhout, "In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm (Extended Version)" (tier 5)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)
